original_question: For Niederreiter-Kronecker hybrid sequences z_n = (x_n, {n alpha})_{n>=0}, where (x_n)_{n>=0} is a fixed digital s-dimensional sequence generated by matrices with finite rows and ({n alpha})_{n>=0} is a t-dimensional Kronecker sequence, what is an essentially sharp upper metrical bound for the discrepancy that holds for almost all alpha?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Open Problem 12 (p. 11): "Give an essentially sharp upper metrical bound for the discrepancy of Niederreiter-Kronecker sequences z_n = (x_n, {n alpha})_{n>=0} where (x_n)_{n>=0} is a given digital s-dimensional sequence generated by matrices with finite rows, and ({n alpha})_{n>=0} is a t-dimensional Kronecker sequence, which is valid for almost all alpha."
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the correct target almost exactly: it identifies the right hybrid class (Niederreiter-Kronecker sequences), the correct decomposition z_n = (x_n, {n alpha}), the finite-row condition on the digital component, the fact that the digital sequence is fixed while the Kronecker parameter alpha is metrical, and that the paper asks for an upper discrepancy bound valid for almost all alpha. It also stays at the general level of Open Problem 12 rather than drifting into the more specific special case of Open Problem 13.
missing_details: The paper's digital component is a digital sequence over Z_q for a prime base q, generated by matrices C_1, ..., C_s in Z_q^{N x N}; this ambient finite field/base data is implicit in your draft and should be stated to make the question stand-alone.
The finite-row hypothesis should be defined explicitly: each row of each generating matrix has only finitely many nonzero entries.
The discrepancy in the paper is the ordinary discrepancy D_N of the first N points z_0, ..., z_{N-1} in [0,1)^{s+t}, not star discrepancy.
The quantifiers s, t in N should be stated explicitly, and the sequence x_n should be described as fixed in advance, with the metric statement ranging only over alpha.
The metrical phrase 'for almost all alpha' should be tied to Lebesgue measure on the Kronecker parameter space.
The hybrid-sequence ambient space [0,1)^{s+t} and the notation {n alpha} for the componentwise fractional part should be made explicit.
The paper asks only for the finite-row digital case here; the harder infinite-row case is mentioned separately as a future direction and should not be folded into this question.

The paper does not state a specific candidate order in Open Problem 12, so the refined question should ask to determine such an essentially optimal order rather than presupposing a particular exponent or log-log factor.
refined_question: Let q be a prime, and let x_n = S(C_1, ..., C_s) be a fixed s-dimensional digital sequence over Z_q generated by matrices C_1, ..., C_s in Z_q^{N x N}, each of whose rows has only finitely many nonzero entries. For alpha in R^t, let ({n alpha})_{n>=0} be the t-dimensional Kronecker sequence obtained by taking componentwise fractional parts, and form the Niederreiter-Kronecker hybrid sequence z_n = (x_n, {n alpha}) in [0,1)^{s+t}. Determine an upper metrical bound, of essentially optimal order in N, for the discrepancy D_N of the first N points z_0, ..., z_{N-1} that holds for Lebesgue-almost every alpha.
justification: This is the exact open problem your draft is aiming at: Section 3, Open Problem 12 (p. 11) states essentially the same question verbatim. The surrounding discussion in Section 3 says that Niederreiter-Kronecker sequences are the 'next more general step' after Halton-Kronecker sequences and that one should first treat the finite-row digital case; this is why the finite-row restriction is paper-critical. The nearby context also defines what a hybrid sequence is (Section 3, p. 9), while Section 1 supplies the paper's discrepancy notation and the construction of digital sequences over Z_q (pp. 1-3). Theorem 3.1 (p. 9) gives the motivating metrical upper bound for Halton-Kronecker sequences, but Open Problem 12 itself is the nearest official formulation and should not be replaced by the more specific one-dimensional special case in Open Problem 13 (p. 11).
